html:
A yearly cycle of six trade fairs held in four towns of the County of Champagne, in northeastern France: Troyes, Provins, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube. They flourished in the 1100s and 1200s and were the main meeting place of European trade.

Champagne lay between the two richest regions of Europe, Flanders and northern Italy. Flemish merchants brought woollen cloth. Italians brought silk, spices, alum and dyes from the Mediterranean and the East, by way of Venice and Genoa. The counts of Champagne kept the roads safe and enforced contracts.

The fairs became a clearing house for money. Merchants settled debts at the end of each fair, and Italian bankers developed bills of exchange and credit there, methods later used by banks such as the Medici Bank.

They declined around 1300, after the French crown took over Champagne and taxed trade, war with Flanders cut the cloth trade, and Italian ships began sailing straight to Bruges. Later fairs at Geneva, Lyon and Piacenza took up the role. In the north, the Hanseatic League ran its own network.
